edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SPORT + SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY
edition.deck: Elections, protest and security lead the agenda, alongside scrutiny of UK policy and developments across Denmark.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritised consequential developments and strong reporting, grouping coverage of shared events. The RAF Fairford story keeps the alleged threat and possible foreign involvement clearly attributed; the Danish stories are translated and grouped by their domestic significance.

content.headline: Brazil’s Flávio Bolsonaro leads Lula after shock first-round election win
content.shortHeadline: Flávio Bolsonaro takes first-round lead in Brazil election
content.standfirst: The far-right candidate has a narrow lead over Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ahead of their 25 October runoff. The result also gives Jair Bolsonaro’s allies a stronger foothold in Congress.

image.caption: Flávio Bolsonaro celebrates after leading the first round of Brazil’s presidential election.

sources.originalTitle: Flávio Bolsonaro poised to win Brazilian presidency after shock first-round victory
Far right on the march and Lula’s failures: key drivers of Flávio Bolsonaro’s Brazil surge

segments.body: Flávio Bolsonaro received 47.03% of the vote to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s 45.16%, leaving the incumbent with ground to make up before the 25 October runoff. No first-round runner-up has won Brazil’s presidency since the return of democracy in 1985, though analysts say the contest is not settled.

perspectives.body: Analysts cited in the Guardian point to evangelical networks, voters’ concerns about crime and frustration over everyday costs as factors behind the far-right showing. They also say Lula’s campaign focused less on issues such as food prices and insecurity than some voters wanted.

segments.title: A stronger Bolsonaro bloc
segments.body: The result extends beyond the presidential race: Jair Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party won the largest Senate caucus, and several members of his family and allies gained seats. Political scientist Miguel Lago told the Guardian the result showed the far right had put down deep roots in Brazilian society.

content.headline: Trump says a threat prompted US bombers to leave RAF Fairford
content.shortHeadline: Trump says threat led US to move bombers from RAF Fairford
content.standfirst: The US president confirmed an unspecified threat led to the aircraft’s withdrawal from the Gloucestershire base. Who made it and what it involved remain unclear, as police continue their investigation.

image.caption: Donald Trump says a threat led the US to move bombers from RAF Fairford.

sources.originalTitle: Trump says 'threat' led US to pull bombers from RAF Fairford
What prompted the US bombers to leave RAF Fairford?
All the signs that Iran was behind RAF Fairford ‘terror plot’

segments.body: Donald Trump said the US moved its bombers from RAF Fairford because of “some threats”. The Pentagon confirmed the aircraft had returned to US home stations. Trump said Washington knew who made the threat but did not identify them or explain its nature.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s security correspondent reports that the withdrawal followed a serious incident near the base and says officials have not disclosed what intelligence prompted the move. UK officials have described an ongoing threat from Iran, while Iran denies involvement.

segments.title: An investigation, not a conclusion
segments.body: Six men arrested in connection with suspected activity near the base have been released on bail. Counter Terrorism Policing says it is considering all possible lines of inquiry, including potential foreign-state involvement. Experts quoted by the i Paper offered theories about criminal proxies, but the suspects’ intentions and any link to Iran have not been established.

content.headline: France braces for nationwide school protests after injuries and arrests
content.shortHeadline: France faces fresh school protests after injuries and mass arrests
content.standfirst: Student groups are calling for a national day of action over overcrowded and poorly maintained schools. The protests have brought serious injuries, thousands of arrests and sharply differing accounts of the police response.

image.caption: Police face a protesting student in Bordeaux during demonstrations on Monday.

sources.originalTitle: France braces for national day of school protests after injuries and mass arrests
France braces for national day of school protests as boy loses hand

segments.body: France is preparing for nationwide demonstrations after a week of school blockades and protests. The BBC reports at least 190 students injured and more than 5,000 people arrested since the movement began. A 15-year-old boy lost a hand during a confrontation in Lens; the circumstances are under investigation.

perspectives.body: The Guardian details students’ demands, including replacement teachers, shorter school days and repairs to deteriorating buildings. It reports that a separate investigation is under way after a pupil in Tours lost sight in one eye; the prosecutor said the injury was consistent with a rubber bullet.

segments.title: Competing claims over the response
segments.body: The government says it has announced measures to address students’ concerns while rejecting violence. Student organisers and unions say the response has been excessive and the proposals too vague. The government says hundreds of schools have been wholly or partly closed as protests and blockades spread.

content.headline: India protests after millions of names are removed from voter lists
content.shortHeadline: Protests grow in India over 130 million names removed from voter lists
content.standfirst: Opposition parties and demonstrators say eligible voters may have been wrongly excluded in a nationwide review. The election commission and the governing BJP deny that the process was designed to favour the government.

image.caption: Demonstrators in India protest the removal of names from voter lists.

sources.originalTitle: Millioner af navne er udeladt af vælgerlister - nu vokser protesterne i verdens største demokrati

segments.body: Around 130 million names have been left off provisional voter lists during an Indian election commission review. Thousands of people protested in Delhi and Mumbai, calling for election commission chief Gyanesh Kumar to resign. The commission says it has asked staff to identify eligible voters missing from the lists and help them register.

segments.title: A dispute reaching the courts
segments.body: The Supreme Court has declined to suspend Kumar while it considers a case relating to his leadership; it has not ruled on the allegations. Critics say the exclusions risk weakening confidence in the voting process. Police have restricted gatherings in Delhi and detained protesters, with one student alleging officers used force.

content.headline: Ukraine says strikes have damaged Russian oil capacity as attacks continue
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine claims strikes hit half of Russia’s oil refining capacity
content.standfirst: Kyiv says attacks have damaged more than half of Russia’s refining capacity; Moscow has not published its own damage figures. The war also brought civilian deaths in Kharkiv and further reported attacks on infrastructure.

image.caption: Smoke rises from a Moscow oil refinery after a reported Ukrainian drone attack.

sources.originalTitle: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv claims half of Russia’s oil refining capacity destroyed
Ukraine sender 650 droner mod Moskva

segments.body: Ukraine’s defence ministry says long-range strikes have hit 51% of Russia’s oil refining capacity. President Vladimir Putin acknowledged that attacks had partly damaged the economy, saying they had cost about 1% of GDP. Russia has not released figures on damage to its oil infrastructure.

segments.title: Attacks on people and infrastructure
segments.body: Officials said Russian bombs killed six people and injured nearly 60 in Kharkiv. Ukraine’s president also said Russian drones struck a civilian grain ship in the Black Sea; Romanian authorities reported two crew members died when a ship caught fire and sank. Separately, Moscow’s mayor claimed Ukraine sent 650 drones towards the region overnight, with 105 intercepted; the fate of the others was unclear. A regional official in Ukraine said a Russian strike damaged a bridge, injuring two people.

content.headline: Japan’s prime minister condemns alleged killing of woman by US Marine on Okinawa
content.shortHeadline: Japan PM condemns alleged killing by US Marine on Okinawa
content.standfirst: A US Marine has been arrested on suspicion of killing a woman in Naha, prompting renewed anger over the military presence on Okinawa. The suspect denies the allegations, and the investigation continues.

image.caption: A US Marine is escorted from a police station after his arrest in Okinawa.

sources.originalTitle: Japan PM leads outcry after US Marine arrested over alleged killing of woman on Okinawa

segments.body: Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, called the alleged crime “heinous” and urged US military authorities to enforce discipline. Police arrested Marine Devin Ballard on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi and stealing her belongings. Ballard denies the allegations; if convicted, he could face life imprisonment or the death penalty.

segments.title: A longstanding source of tension
segments.body: Okinawa hosts most of the US troops stationed in Japan and most of the country’s US military facilities. The island’s governor said the case heightened local fears, while the US military said it recognised residents’ concern. The planned relocation of Futenma air station has faced years of local opposition.

content.headline: Trump faces weak poll numbers and criticism over taxpayer-funded ads
content.shortHeadline: Trump’s low approval and campaign moves raise midterm pressure
content.standfirst: Polls cited by the Guardian put the president’s approval at a new low, while his campaign appearances and government-funded promotional ads have drawn criticism, including from Republicans. The midterms are due next month.

image.caption: Donald Trump speaks to reporters before travelling to Nebraska.

sources.originalTitle: Trump approval ratings plummet to new low, polls show
Trump’s chaotic speech with bribes and threats shows he is the Democrats’ best asset
Trump says he will stop using taxpayer funds for ads after bipartisan pushback

segments.body: A Reuters/Ipsos poll put Donald Trump’s approval at 32%, a record low in that survey, with weaker support among independents and Latino voters. Trump dismissed questions about his ratings. A separate NBC News/Telemundo poll found 59% of Latino voters preferred a Democratic-controlled Congress.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s account of Trump’s campaign events describes threats to withhold federal funding from Ohio if voters elect a Democratic governor and promises of payments to voters that would require congressional approval. It argues his appearances could undermine Republican candidates.

segments.title: Bipartisan objections to public spending
segments.body: Trump said he would stop using taxpayer money for television ads promoting himself and his policies, after criticism from Democrats and Republicans over whether public funds could be used for political advertising. He said he would pay for future ads himself and with money raised by his political action committee.

content.headline: Quebec separatists projected to win provincial election, renewing unity test
content.shortHeadline: Quebec separatists projected to win, reviving independence question
content.standfirst: The Parti Québécois is projected to take a minority victory and return to power for the first time since 2014. Its leader has pledged an independence referendum, though polls suggest the proposal has limited support.

image.caption: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, whose Parti Québécois was projected to win Quebec’s election.

sources.originalTitle: Separatist party projected to win Quebec election, adding new test to Canada's unity

segments.body: Canadian media projected a minority win for the sovereigntist Parti Québécois, making Paul St-Pierre Plamondon the incoming premier. The party has promised a referendum on independence after Donald Trump leaves office. Polls cited by the BBC show about 30% of Quebecers support independence.

segments.title: Tensions with Ottawa
segments.body: Plamondon has also pledged to challenge federal policy on immigration and reduce the monarchy’s role in Quebec. His plan to withdraw funding from the lieutenant-governor’s office could face legal obstacles, as the office has a constitutional role including granting royal assent to provincial laws.

content.headline: MPs call for independent review of financial watchdog after whistleblower’s’ ‘tr
content.shortHeadline: MPs seek review of FCA handling of whistleblower who later died
content.standfirst: Simon Andriesz’s family said he took his own life in Thailand, with no suggestion of foul play. MPs are calling for an independent review of how the Financial Conduct Authority handled his complaints and allegations of retaliation.

image.caption: Simon Andriesz, a former senior employee of BGC Partners.

sources.originalTitle: MPs call for investigation after Lutnick-Epstein whistleblower dies

segments.body: UK MPs have called for an independent assessment of the Financial Conduct Authority’s handling of Simon Andriesz, a former BGC Partners employee who died in Thailand last month. His family said he took his own life and there was no suggestion of foul play. Andriesz had raised concerns with the FCA and other bodies about alleged business links between Howard Lutnick and Jeffrey Epstein, and alleged misconduct at BGC.

segments.title: Dispute over the regulator’s response
segments.body: Andriesz said he felt “thoroughly let down” by the FCA, which had previously told him there was insufficient evidence of retaliation by BGC. The firm denied retaliating against him and denied an allegation that bonus-pool money had been misused. The FCA says it has asked newly appointed board member Lea Paterson to review its interactions with Andriesz and identify lessons.

content.headline: Cancer diagnoses among under-50s rise for several types, study finds
content.shortHeadline: Study finds sharp rises in several cancers among under-50s
content.standfirst: An international analysis found significant increases in early-onset cancers in England, the US and the Netherlands. Researchers say risk factors and earlier diagnosis may both contribute, and that the reasons are not yet fully understood.

image.caption: A patient undergoes a CT scan.

sources.originalTitle: Cancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international study finds

segments.body: A World Cancer Research Fund analysis found significant rises in seven types of cancer among under-50s in England, five in the US and four in the Netherlands. In England, prostate cancer diagnoses in this age group quadrupled between 2001 and 2023; bowel, kidney and uterine cancer rates also rose sharply. Cancer remains much more common among older people.

segments.title: Causes and next steps remain uncertain
segments.body: Researchers say obesity, diet, exercise, alcohol, smoking and environmental exposures could contribute, but increased awareness and earlier diagnosis also affect the figures. They say better detection does not explain the whole trend. King’s College London is to lead a 250,000-person trial examining the rise in bowel cancer among younger adults.

content.headline: Greens face backlash after adopting policy calling Zionism a form of racism
content.shortHeadline: Green Party policy on Zionism sparks international backlash
content.standfirst: The English and Welsh Greens’ conference adopted a policy equating Zionism with racism, prompting criticism from European Green parties and debate over the party’s policymaking. The motion passed with support from a small fraction of members.

image.caption: Zack Polanski speaks at the Green Party conference in Brighton.

sources.originalTitle: Green party of England and Wales facing international ostracism over ‘Zionism is racism’ vote
Zack Polanski may regret not using his influence when Greens needed him to act

segments.body: A binding motion at the Green Party of England and Wales conference said Zionism should be treated as a form of racism and backed one democratic Palestinian state with equal rights. Four of the party’s five MPs opposed it. The European Green Party said the motion conflicted with its support for a two-state solution and called for clarification from the party leadership.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s analysis argues that party leader Zack Polanski’s absence from the debate and vote has drawn criticism, even though he could not have changed the party’s member-led decision alone. It notes the motion passed by 209 votes, with 1,022 members supporting it.

segments.title: Criticism and debate within the party
segments.body: The German Greens’ co-leader called the motion unacceptable, and a longstanding Green member resigned from an Amnesty International UK charitable trust role over it, accusing the party of failing to confront antisemitism. Green leader Zack Polanski said antisemitism and criticism of Israel must remain distinct. The vote has also intensified questions about how the party makes policy as its membership grows.

content.headline: SEND support scheme faces staffing concerns despite £1.8bn funding
content.shortHeadline: Staff shortages threaten promised specialist support for SEND pupils
content.standfirst: Councils, school leaders and a charity warn that shortages of educational psychologists and therapists could limit a new three-year scheme for pupils with special educational needs. Ministers say rollout is phased and capacity-building has begun.

image.caption: Schools minister Georgia Gould promoted the “experts at hand” scheme.

sources.originalTitle: SEND pupils’ extra support at risk with schools unable to access specialist staff

segments.body: The Government’s £1.8bn “experts at hand” programme is intended to give mainstream schools better access to educational psychologists, speech and language therapists, occupational therapists and specialist teachers. At least 36 councils have raised concerns about recruiting enough staff, according to analysis by Schools Week reported by the i Paper.

segments.title: Government says rollout is under way
segments.body: A specialist charity said it had received no firm plans from the 20 councils it works with, while school leaders warned that long waits for support affect pupils and add pressure on staff. The Department for Education said the programme began last month and will expand over three years, acknowledging that recruiting and training specialists will take time.

content.headline: Nurseries to face tighter rules on staff phones and children’s photos
content.shortHeadline: Nurseries to get new phone and photo safeguards after abuse case
content.standfirst: Draft guidance is expected to restrict personal devices in childcare areas, limit routine photographs and strengthen checks on work devices. The changes follow a serious abuse case and concerns over children’s images being misused.

image.caption: New guidance is expected to curb nursery staff use of digital devices around children.

sources.originalTitle: Nursery staff to be banned from using phones after ‘chilling’ child abuse case

segments.body: Government guidance expected this month will tell nursery staff, childminders and visitors not to use personal phones and digital devices in childcare areas. Settings are expected to use a designated work device and limit routine photographs to one per child per day, with parents able to request extra images during settling-in.

segments.title: Safeguarding and implementation
segments.body: The proposals follow the case of Vincent Chan, who was jailed after abusing children at a north London nursery. Guidance is also expected to require parental permission for images, checks of work devices and caution over sharing identifiable photographs online or uploading them to AI tools. A nursery workers’ union representative warned that staffing pressures and uneven training could hinder implementation.

content.headline: Barrister says prosecutions of small-boat pilots target asylum seekers, not sm
content.shortHeadline: Barrister says small-boat laws risk prosecuting asylum seekers
content.standfirst: A defence barrister argues that recent prosecutions punish vulnerable people who take the tiller rather than dismantling smuggling networks. Ministers say enforcement is disrupting crossings, which remain a point of sharp disagreement.

image.caption: A dinghy carrying 165 asylum seekers crossed the Channel in July.

sources.originalTitle: I represented the pilot of a mega-dinghy. Why Channel migrants are still arriving

segments.body: Audrey Mogan, who represented a 19-year-old sentenced to more than two years in prison for piloting an overcrowded Channel dinghy, says the law is being used against asylum seekers who may have had little control over the boat. Her client admitted endangering lives during the crossing; she says he had no control over overcrowding or safety equipment.

segments.title: Government defends enforcement
segments.body: Mogan and the Refugee Council argue that prosecuting people who have fled conflict will not disrupt smuggling gangs and that safe, legal routes are needed. The Government says crossings are down and its joint efforts have prevented more than 48,000 attempts and seized 1,100 boats and engines since the election.

content.headline: Avanti’s return to public ownership will not quickly fix delays, experts warn
content.shortHeadline: Avanti nationalisation unlikely to quickly fix delays or fares
content.standfirst: Experts say bottlenecks and signalling problems on the West Coast Main Line are major causes of disruption and will not be solved by changing the operator’s ownership. They also caution that public ownership alone will not cut fares.

image.caption: An Avanti West Coast train, whose on-time performance was the worst among operators last year.

sources.originalTitle: The UK’s worst rail firm is being nationalised. But don’t expect improvements soon

segments.body: Avanti West Coast is due to return to public ownership in March after recording the lowest on-time rate of any operator in 2025–26 and the second-highest cancellation rate. The rail regulator attributed 66% of its delayed minutes to Network Rail issues, including disruption on the congested West Coast Main Line.

segments.title: Infrastructure and fares remain open questions
segments.body: Rail experts say the line’s capacity constraints and bottlenecks need investment, and that nationalisation alone is no quick fix. Network Rail has a £400m improvement programme due to finish by March 2029, but one expert described much of it as maintenance rather than a major expansion of capacity. Experts also say state ownership will not automatically lower fares.

content.headline: Tories pledge £10bn UK air defence network, far below expert estimates
content.shortHeadline: Tories propose £10bn air shield as experts cite much higher cost
content.standfirst: The Conservatives say an integrated system of radar, command technology and interceptors would protect UK infrastructure and bases. Experts have put the cost of a full-scale shield at up to £80bn or more.

image.caption: A Royal Navy Type 45 destroyer, one of the UK assets able to intercept ballistic missiles.

sources.originalTitle: Badenoch promises ‘Britannia Dome’ missile shield
Tories pledge £10bn 'Britannia Shield' air defence system

segments.body: The Conservatives have proposed a £10bn “Britannia Shield” linking radar, command systems, interceptor missiles and counter-drone weapons. The party says it would fund the programme through its plans to raise defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030 and welfare reform.

perspectives.body: The i Paper reports that the proposed price is far below previous estimates: General Sir Richard Barrons told a parliamentary committee that an entry-level system could cost about £80bn over ten years. The paper also reports that the Defence Investment Plan allocated £790m for integrated air and missile defence.

segments.title: A campaign pledge, with political dispute over the cost
segments.body: The Conservatives say a basic system could be in place during their first term. Labour says the government is increasing defence spending and investing £1bn in air defences. The BBC reports the existing Defence Investment Plan includes more than £350m to double the Army’s Sky Sabre systems; the parties dispute their records and priorities.

content.headline: Frederiksen proposes help desk to unblock local projects held up by rules
content.shortHeadline: Frederiksen proposes new office to help local projects through red
content.standfirst: The government plans a Nykøbing Falster office to help municipalities and local groups navigate barriers to development. The opposition says simplifying the rules would be better than creating another office.

image.caption: Mette Frederiksen visited the sauna and bathing club in Nysted last week.

sources.originalTitle: Hjælp fra regeringen: Bøvl og regler må ikke stoppe lokale ildsjæle

segments.body: Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen says the government will establish an office in Nykøbing Falster to help municipalities and local groups move projects through state processes. She cited plans including a sauna extension in Nysted that was rejected under coastal-protection rules, alongside projects involving industry, housing and energy.

Frederiksen says some projects may require changes to planning rules or additional funding, while others could benefit from a fresh assessment. Former minister Morten Dahlin welcomed the stated aims but argued that simpler legislation and more local freedom would be preferable to a new office.

content.headline: Police admit they should have called neighbour after failing to attend woman’s
content.shortHeadline: Police admit error after failing to attend woman’s emergency call
content.standfirst: Fyn Police say they should have told a caller they would not be coming to his neighbour’s flat, where 23-year-old Cecilie Voller Kjærulff was later found dead. The force says its assessment at the time was not itself an error.

image.caption: Cecilie Voller Kjærulff, who died in her flat in Odense.

sources.originalTitle: Nabo ringede forgæves: Politiet erkender fejl i sag om 23-årigs død

segments.body: Anders Østerby called police twice after hearing worrying noises from his upstairs neighbour’s flat in Odense. Officers told him they would attend, but no one came. Cecilie Voller Kjærulff, 23, was found dead the next day. A post-mortem concluded she probably died from an overdose of medication prescribed for bipolar disorder.

segments.title: New procedures after police review
segments.body: Fyn Police say staff should have contacted the caller when they decided not to attend because other reports took priority. The force says it has tightened call-centre procedures and questioning guidance, but maintains its original assessment was reasonable based on the information available at the time. Her parents remain critical; experts told DR she would likely have survived if she had reached hospital when the neighbour called.

content.headline: Copenhagen’s Ring 3 to widen as speed limit falls to 90km/h
content.shortHeadline: Ring 3 around Copenhagen to widen, with lower speed limit
content.standfirst: The 17-kilometre motorway is set to gain a fourth lane in each direction on most of its route, with noise-reducing asphalt and a lower speed limit. Work is planned to start in 2027.

image.caption: Ring 3 around Copenhagen is set to be widened on most of its route.

sources.originalTitle: En af Danmarks mest trafikerede motorveje skal nu udvides

segments.body: The agreement on the infrastructure plan calls for most of Ring 3 to be widened from three to four lanes in each direction, using the hard shoulder as a lane, and for noise-reducing asphalt to be laid. The speed limit will fall from 110km/h to 90km/h for safety reasons.

Ring 3 carries more than 145,000 vehicles a day. The road directorate estimates the asphalt could reduce noise by three to four decibels for about 40% of homes along the route. A local mayor welcomed the noise measures but said a lower limit of 80km/h could reduce noise further. Work is scheduled to begin in 2027 and finish between 2029 and 2030.

content.headline: Man dies after stabbing near Herning; no arrests made
content.shortHeadline: Man, 57, dies after stabbing near Herning
content.standfirst: A 57-year-old man died after being stabbed at his home in Hammerum. Police say no one has been arrested and there is currently no information linking the killing to a separate gang conflict investigation.

sources.originalTitle: 57-årig mand død efter knivstikkeri nær Herning

segments.body: Mid- and West Jutland Police say the man was stabbed at his home in Hammerum near Herning on Monday evening. Attempts to save him were unsuccessful and he was declared dead about an hour later. No one has been arrested.

Police said there is currently no information linking the killing to a conflict between criminal groups in Herning, which they are also investigating. The circumstances of the stabbing remain unclear.

content.headline: Copenhagen seaplane gets temporary permit as search for new harbour location
content.shortHeadline: Copenhagen seaplane permit extended while new location is sought
content.standfirst: A committee voted to extend the seaplane’s environmental permit temporarily, postponing a final decision as the operator is asked to find another harbour location. The proposal still needs a vote in the city council.

image.caption: A seaplane serving the Copenhagen–Aarhus route, whose future remains undecided.

sources.originalTitle: Vandflyversag tager ny drejning: Alternativet kalder det et 'kæmpe svigt'

segments.body: Copenhagen’s climate, environment and technology committee voted to extend Nordic Seaplanes’ current environmental approval temporarily, allowing it to operate until mid-2027 while it and the city administration seek an alternative location. The committee did not grant permanent approval.

Alternativeet’s Karoline Lindgaard called the proposal a “major green betrayal”, arguing that the service creates noise and pollution for few passengers. Supporters said the extension gives the company time to find a new site and consider a transition to electric aircraft. City council is due to consider the matter on 5 November.

content.headline: Pandora opens major Vietnam factory beside Lego site
content.shortHeadline: Pandora opens Vietnam factory beside Lego’s global facility
content.standfirst: The jewellery company says its new factory near Ho Chi Minh City will produce up to 60 million pieces a year and employ 7,000 people when fully operational. It is Pandora’s first factory outside Thailand.

image.caption: Pandora and Lego executives at the site of the new Pandora factory in Vietnam.

sources.originalTitle: Millioner Milliarder: To danske topdirektører er blevet naboer på den anden side af Jorden

segments.body: Pandora has opened a factory near Ho Chi Minh City built at a cost of about 1bn Danish kroner. The company says it will be capable of making 60 million pieces of jewellery a year and employing 7,000 people when fully operational. A Lego factory occupies the neighbouring site.

Pandora says the facility will help meet its growth ambitions. The report presents the neighbouring Danish companies as part of a wider pattern of Danish businesses investing in Vietnam; a visit by Vietnam’s president to Denmark is also expected in the coming weeks.

content.headline: Skive faces criticism over royal visit meal at restaurant without agreement
content.shortHeadline: Skive criticised for booking royal visit meal at restaurant without
content.standfirst: A local councillor and 3F criticised the municipality’s choice of restaurant for the King and Queen’s visit, citing the absence of a collective agreement. The mayor says the location was chosen for its proximity to a new bathing facility.

image.caption: King Frederik and Queen Mary are due to visit Skive on Friday.

sources.originalTitle: Kongeparret er inviteret på restaurant uden overenskomst: Politiker kalder det forkert

segments.body: Skive Municipality has arranged a meal at Hereford Beefstouw for the King and Queen during the town’s 700th-anniversary celebrations. SF councillor Mie Johansen said the municipality should set an example by choosing a restaurant with a collective agreement. 3F has also criticised the choice, according to TV 2.

Mayor Alfred Brunsgaard said the restaurant was selected because it is close to the Fjordbadet bathing facility, which the royal couple are due to open. He said the municipality cannot require a restaurant to have a collective agreement and expects to discuss the issue with 3F.

content.headline: Village residents recruit new shopkeeper through social-media campaign
content.shortHeadline: Danish village finds shopkeeper after unusual community campaign
content.standfirst: After its Spar shop closed, residents bought the building and launched a playful online search for a new shopkeeper. The new operator hopes to reopen the refurbished store by the end of November.

image.caption: Øster Tørslev residents promoted their search for a new shopkeeper online.

sources.originalTitle: Desperat landsby tog utraditionel metode i brug. Nu har de fundet købmand

segments.body: Residents of Øster Tørslev near Randers formed a company to buy the village’s former Spar shop after it closed. They then posted a reality-show-style recruitment video called “Village Seeks Shopkeeper”. The campaign attracted more and stronger applicants than the chain typically receives, Dagrofa said.

The community is working with Dagrofa on a resident-supported shop. New shopkeeper Thomas Dalsgaard Ettrup said he shared the residents’ aim of developing the area and making the business sustainable. The group hopes to open the renovated store by late November.

content.headline: Elfyn Evans wins first world rally title after Solberg crashes late
content.shortHeadline: Evans wins first world rally title after Solberg’s late crash
content.standfirst: Elfyn Evans became the first British men’s world rally champion in 25 years after Oliver Solberg went off the track with two turns left on the final stage in Sardinia.

image.caption: Elfyn Evans (centre) pictured with British world rally champions Colin McRae (left) and Richard Burns (right).

sources.originalTitle: How Evans defied history to join rallying greats

segments.body: Evans was preparing for another runners-up finish as he waited for Solberg to complete the final stage of Rally Italia Sardegna. Solberg, who was close to securing the title, went off the track with two turns remaining, allowing Evans to claim his first World Rally Championship crown.

segments.title: A long-awaited breakthrough
segments.body: The 37-year-old from north Wales had finished second in the championship five times, including by just four points to Sébastien Ogier in 2025. Evans and co-driver Scott Martin took a 21-point lead into the final rally despite winning only two of the previous 12 events.

content.headline: Medvedev defaulted after hitting spectator with ball at China Open
content.shortHeadline: Medvedev defaulted after hitting a spectator with a ball
content.standfirst: Daniil Medvedev was disqualified while trailing Novak Djokovic in their China Open semi-final. He apologised and said he hoped to speak to the spectator, whose condition was not reported.

image.caption: Daniil Medvedev was disqualified after striking a spectator with a ball.

sources.originalTitle: Medvedev disqualified for hitting spectator with ball

segments.body: Medvedev trailed Djokovic 7-5, 5-3 when he swiped at the ball in frustration after Djokovic hit a winner. It struck a spectator in the front row, who was helped out of the arena while holding his eye. The offence was serious enough for the umpire and an ATP official to default Medvedev immediately.

segments.title: An apology and a place in the final
segments.body: Medvedev said he was “terribly sorry” and hoped to apologise in person, adding that the spectator’s wellbeing was what mattered most to him. Djokovic expressed sympathy for both the spectator and Medvedev, and said he did not believe the act was intentional. Medvedev will lose the points and prize money earned in Beijing.

segments.title: Djokovic advances
segments.body: The default ended a close match in which Djokovic saved 16 of the 18 break points he faced. He will play Alex de Minaur in Tuesday’s final.

content.headline: Gauff condemns racist abuse after China Open win
content.shortHeadline: Gauff condemns racist abuse after China Open win
content.standfirst: Coco Gauff said she received racist comments and messages online after stopping a point because of a flickering court light during her win over Sun Xinran in Beijing.

image.caption: Coco Gauff said she received racist abuse online after her China Open win.

sources.originalTitle: Gauff condemns racist abuse after China Open win

segments.body: Gauff halted play while serving at 4-5 in the first set, saying a light in the court’s side panels was flickering. Sun had thought she hit a winner. Gauff held serve, took the set and went on to win 7-5, 6-1, reaching the last 16.

segments.title: Abuse online
segments.body: Gauff said Sun understood and accepted her apology, but she later replied to a social media post containing racist language. “You can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist,” she wrote. The report says female players received more than 12,000 abusive posts and messages on social media in 2025.

content.headline: ECB may consider funding West Indies women's Test before Ashes
content.shortHeadline: ECB may help fund West Indies women's Test before the Ashes
content.standfirst: The ECB says it would consider funding a planned women’s Test in the West Indies if necessary. The tour is not under threat, but the financial uncertainty comes as England seek red-ball preparation before the Ashes.

sources.originalTitle: ECB will 'look at' funding Windies Test if needed

segments.body: The West Indies Test is scheduled as part of a multi-format series in spring 2027, before England’s bid to regain the Ashes. After Cricket West Indies announced cost-saving measures, including cuts to player contracts, ECB chair Richard Thompson said his board would “look at” providing funding if the issue arose.

segments.title: Preparation and uncertainty
segments.body: There have been no discussions between the boards about cancelling the Test, and the wider tour, including three T20s and three one-day internationals, is not under threat. Dates and venues are still to be confirmed. England have played only one Test since the last Ashes, making the planned match a potentially important warm-up before the Headingley Test in June 2027.

content.headline: Gloucester thrash Harlequins as Bristol underline top-four ambitions
content.shortHeadline: Gloucester thrash Quins as Bristol make a top-four statement
content.standfirst: Gloucester inflicted Harlequins’ heaviest league defeat in 26 years, while Bristol beat Northampton 34-26. Bath also won, leaving three teams unbeaten after the first two rounds of the Prem.

image.caption: Gloucester, Bristol and Bath are the three teams with two wins after the Prem’s opening rounds.

sources.originalTitle: Salty celebrations, questionable signings and Test bolters - Prem talking points

segments.body: Harlequins lost 48-0 to Gloucester, conceding 17 penalties and making only two entries into the opposition 22. Coach Jason Gilmore called the performance “totally unacceptable”. The report says injuries and a struggling forward pack leave Quins needing several players to step up.

segments.title: Bristol build momentum
segments.body: Bristol beat Northampton 34-26 in front of a crowd of 20,756, around 5,000 higher than at the same fixture last year. Louis Rees-Zammit has scored four tries in the first two rounds, and Bristol face a demanding run of fixtures against other sides with top-four ambitions.

segments.title: England selection possibilities
segments.body: England coach Steve Borthwick was at Bath’s win over Exeter, where the report highlights the scrum work of Beno Obano and Will Stuart as possible options for England’s bench. Gloucester fly-half Charlie Atkinson is another player the piece suggests could come into contention, although his goal-kicking may count against him.

content.headline: Kane could equal Shilton's 125-cap England record if he plays
content.shortHeadline: Kane could equal England's 125-cap record if he plays
content.standfirst: Harry Kane is already England’s record goalscorer, with 89 goals, and could draw level with Peter Shilton’s appearance record against the Czech Republic. Former internationals agree he is an England great, but differ on how he ranks among the very best.

image.caption: Harry Kane, England’s record goalscorer, could equal Peter Shilton’s 125-cap record if he plays.

sources.originalTitle: England's greatest international? Kane is now a serious contender

segments.body: Kane will equal Shilton’s 125 caps if he features in England’s Nations League meeting with the Czech Republic at Wembley. He has 124 appearances and is already the men’s team’s leading scorer with 89 goals, 36 clear of Wayne Rooney.

segments.title: Greatness and silverware
segments.body: Former England midfielder Danny Murphy said Kane’s goals, professionalism and longevity put him among the country’s greats, while stressing that comparisons depend on era and opinion. Paul Robinson argued that modern players can be undervalued against past icons such as Bobby Moore and Sir Bobby Charlton.

segments.title: The missing trophy
segments.body: Kane has reached two European Championship finals and two World Cup semi-finals without winning a major international trophy. Murphy said that remains the main qualification in the debate, but rejected the idea that Kane alone was responsible for England falling short. The report notes that the 2028 Euros could be another chance to add silverware.

content.headline: Ronaldo's Portugal future uncertain after leaving squad in dispute
content.shortHeadline: Ronaldo's Portugal future uncertain after squad dispute
content.standfirst: Cristiano Ronaldo left Portugal’s camp after learning he would not start against Denmark, following an unused substitute appearance against Norway. Talks are ongoing, and manager Jorge Jesus says the decision to return is Ronaldo’s.

image.caption: A sign outside Benfica’s stadium thanks Cristiano Ronaldo and criticises Jorge Jesus.

sources.originalTitle: A nation divided as Ronaldo left with big decision on Portugal future

segments.body: Ronaldo, Portugal’s captain and record scorer, left the squad after being told he would not start against Denmark. He had been an unused substitute against Norway after warming up, then walked down the tunnel at full-time. Ronaldo later wrote that he would explain his reasons for leaving “in due course”.

segments.title: A divided reaction
segments.body: Jesus has said Ronaldo would be welcome back and that the forward should decide how he wants to end his international career. Some fans and Portuguese media criticised Ronaldo’s actions; others backed him, including on posters in Lisbon attacking Jesus’s handling of the captain. Lisbon fan Maria Ribeiro told BBC Sport it was hard to imagine Portugal without Ronaldo, but wondered whether “maybe this is the time”.

segments.title: What happens next?
segments.body: Ronaldo has 234 caps and 146 goals for Portugal, both world records, but whether he will return remains unresolved. Journalist Marcus Alves told BBC Sport that disputes with several of Portugal’s recent coaches have become a distraction, while Portugal’s results without Ronaldo have been slightly better in the period cited by the report.

content.headline: Bournemouth expect Alex Scott to miss up to eight weeks after England injury
content.shortHeadline: Alex Scott could miss eight weeks after England injury
content.standfirst: Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott is expected to miss six to eight weeks with a quadriceps injury after playing 70 minutes for England against Croatia. The club is reportedly frustrated with how the injury was handled.

image.caption: Alex Scott won his second England cap against Croatia.

sources.originalTitle: Bournemouth unhappy after Scott injured with England

segments.body: Scott withdrew from England’s squad for the Czech Republic match after a scan showed a quadriceps problem. He had felt an issue before the 7-0 win over Croatia but played 70 minutes. Bournemouth are reportedly unhappy with England’s handling of the injury, given the club understood he had been carrying a thigh issue.

segments.title: England's account
segments.body: Thomas Tuchel said Scott had trained fully, completed extra work and received “green lights” from the player and medical staff. He said there was no risk taken by England, adding that Scott had not felt injured even before his scan. Bournemouth expect him to miss the nine games they have scheduled between 10 October and 8 November.

content.headline: Metallica’s Sphere residency turns a rarities set into an immersive epic
content.shortHeadline: Metallica turn Sphere rarities set into an immersive epic
content.standfirst: The band opened its Las Vegas residency with a no-repeat promise and a set spanning decades. The Sphere’s monstrous visuals sometimes compete with the music, but a tight, forceful performance holds its ground.

image.caption: Metallica perform at Sphere in Las Vegas.

sources.originalTitle: Metallica review – metal titans on fine form in spectacular rarities-focused show

segments.body: Metallica launched their 24-show Life Burns Faster residency with a set designed to reward dedicated fans: the band say they will play twice a week without repeating a song within the same week. Rather than rely on a greatest-hits sequence, the opening night moved across their catalogue, from “Now That We’re Dead” and “Lux Æterna” to “The Call of Ktulu” and “Seek and Destroy”.

segments.title: The band against the spectacle
segments.body: The Sphere’s enormous images turn songs into theatrical scenes: during “The Call of Ktulu”, a giant creature stalks a projected Las Vegas; for “Ride the Lightning”, the audience sees the action from an electric chair. At times the scale overwhelms, but the review finds the group’s playing—especially Lars Ulrich’s fluid drumming and James Hetfield’s voice—keeps the show focused.

content.headline: Liz Harris finds a restorative counterpoint to Grouper’s solitude in Helen
content.shortHeadline: Liz Harris finds restoration in Helen’s shared sound
content.standfirst: The ambient musician discusses the return of her dream-pop trio and the relief of making music with friends. A viral track also brought a stark lesson in how easily streaming royalties can be stolen.

image.caption: Liz Harris of Helen and Grouper.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Liz Harris describes Grouper as intensely solitary music, but says the revived trio Helen lets her show a more playful, social side. Making Helen’s new album, Linda’s Head, was “really restorative” while she was dealing with medical difficulties. Its collaborative brightness does not erase the darkness in the songs; it gives that darkness company.

segments.title: The risks of sudden attention
segments.body: Harris says a fraudulent upload of her song “Poison Tree” accrued millions of plays and around six figures before she and her label were able to stop the scam and recover what she was owed. Fake remixes and tracks with matching titles have also required constant attention. The experience, she says, has reinforced her fear of becoming more deeply involved in the music industry.

content.headline: Tom Morello’s first solo rock album turns protest into a family legacy
content.shortHeadline: Tom Morello brings protest and family into solo debut
content.standfirst: On Everyone Gets What They Want, the Rage Against the Machine guitarist renews his political call to action and works with his teenage son. He traces that conviction to his mother, Mary, whose example shaped his activism.

image.caption: Tom Morello during an interview about his new solo album.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Morello on Rage Against the Machine fans turning against him

segments.body: Tom Morello calls Everyone Gets What They Want his first full-length solo rock album, a collection of anti-racist and anti-fascist songs that he describes as a “call to arms”. It features Serj Tankian, Kneecap and Morello’s 15-year-old son Roman, who co-wrote five tracks. Morello says making rebellious music feels like self-care in a dangerous time.

segments.title: A conviction learned at home
segments.body: Morello credits his mother, Mary, with teaching him that ordinary people can change the world. He recalls her taking part in civil-rights and anti-colonial causes and explaining why their family would join the United Farm Workers grape boycott. After her death at 102, he set up a memorial project encouraging people to donate, volunteer and protest in causes she supported.

content.headline: Interpol revisit their New York roots and widen their sound on This Mirror Weigh
content.shortHeadline: Interpol revisit New York and widen their sound
content.standfirst: The band’s eighth album brings fresh arrangements to their familiar angular indie rock. Paul Banks and Daniel Kessler discuss a return to recording in New York, the band’s early scene and their wariness about AI-made art.

image.caption: Paul Banks and Daniel Kessler of Interpol.

sources.originalTitle: Interpol: ‘People romanticise the Noughties music scene. We weren’t all friends’

segments.body: This Mirror Weighs a Ton is presented as a return to form with new textures: ambient and trip-hop elements, piano ballads, woodwind and, for the first time on an Interpol track, acoustic guitar. The band recorded in Manhattan with producer Andrew Wyatt, and bassist Brad Truax joined the writing process as a full member.

segments.title: The scene, remembered differently
segments.body: Paul Banks and Daniel Kessler recall the much-romanticised New York indie scene of the early 2000s with some reservations. Banks says he once pushed back against the idea that its bands were all friends; Kessler recalls wanting to find like-minded peers but rarely seeing that sense of camaraderie. They also argue that artists seek sincerity and expression, not music made merely to be sold.

perspectives.body: Kessler says Interpol’s return to writing in New York brought a sense of history and belonging. Banks, meanwhile, links the new album’s themes to modern life, including war footage he encountered online and questions about how language shapes truth.

content.headline: Soft Cell’s Danceteria becomes a final album after Dave Ball’s death
content.shortHeadline: Soft Cell’s final album closes a long creative partnership
content.standfirst: Marc Almond says he and Dave Ball had finished Danceteria just two days before Ball died in 2025. The album revisits their early-80s New York years, mixing dance-pop exhilaration with memories of a scene later transformed by AIDS.

image.caption: Marc Almond and Dave Ball of Soft Cell.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Soft Cell’s sixth album, Danceteria, is also their last: Marc Almond says he would not make another record under the band’s name without Dave Ball. The pair agreed the album was finished, Almond recalls, two days before Ball died in his sleep at 66 in October 2025, after years of health problems.

segments.title: A city in the music
segments.body: The album looks back to the New York clubs that changed Soft Cell, with Almond describing a world that was dangerous, dark and creatively exuberant. Tracks evoke the rush of nightlife but also its loneliness and the way the city changed as AIDS took its toll. Almond says he felt relief that he and Ball had made the record together, even as he mourns that Ball would not see its release.

content.headline: Jake Xerxes Fussell turns old folk fragments into a coherent, wandering album
content.shortHeadline: Jake Xerxes Fussell makes old songs feel newly travelled
content.standfirst: The North Carolina musician draws on traditional ballads, blues and sea shanties for a subdued record of drifters and uneasy travellers. The review finds a strikingly unified album in those far-flung sources.

sources.originalTitle: The Old Beloved Path

segments.body: On The Old Beloved Path, Jake Xerxes Fussell builds most of the songs from traditional material, from an Irish ballad to a blues standard. His plaintive baritone and fingerpicking sit among harmonica, mandolin and fiddle, with production by Ben Whiteley. The review describes a meditative record that makes an unusually coherent whole from diverse sources.

The songs gather people in motion: sailors, drifters and others looking for a new beginning. Fussell’s “Boll Weevil” turns a familiar blues figure into a dispossessed wanderer, while “Rock Island Line” combines an old nursery rhyme with the skiffle song, becoming a slow-moving travel tune. The review’s point is that these old routes can still lead somewhere unexpected.

content.headline: Elvis Costello’s expanded My Aim Is True traces a gradual transformation
content.shortHeadline: A Costello box set reveals the slow making of My Aim Is True
content.standfirst: The 104-track anniversary edition revisits the making of Costello’s debut, with demos and live recordings that complicate the idea of an overnight breakthrough. The review hears a craftsman finding his voice over time.

sources.originalTitle: My Aim Is True (49th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: The new five-CD edition of My Aim Is True adds demos, live sets and earlier recordings to Elvis Costello’s 1977 debut. Rather than simply celebrating a finished classic, the collection tracks an artist trying out influences and approaches. Its second disc, The Blue Print, is especially revealing: the songs show a capable writer before the punk and new wave character of the album had fully emerged.

segments.title: A voice taking shape
segments.body: The review describes the album’s blend of catchy complaint-rock, musical range and sharp writing, with “Alison” still its emotional centre. Later discs follow Costello’s songs and persona coming into sharper focus, while the final Clover reunion recording is judged more a fan’s keepsake than an essential chapter. Together, the set makes the case for gradual transformation rather than sudden invention.

content.headline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul remains an album of productive contradictions
content.shortHeadline: Rubber Soul’s many versions keep the Beatles classic in flux
content.standfirst: The new deluxe set gathers UK and US editions, alternate mixes and studio outtakes around a record that changed pop’s sense of what an album could be. The review argues there is no single definitive version.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: Rubber Soul marked a shift toward the Beatles treating an album as an artwork in its own right, while they were still racing to meet a release deadline. The new set documents that compressed process through alternate takes, mixes and recording notes. Its UK and US editions also reveal how label decisions produced different versions of the same landmark record.

segments.title: No one real Rubber Soul
segments.body: The review finds pleasure in the set’s contrasts: stereo and mono, the UK and US tracklists, finished songs and outtakes. Small details in the mixes can alter the feel of a performance, but the new remix is not a wholesale reinvention. The larger point is that the album has never been one fixed object; listeners bring their own history to the version they know.

content.headline: Digger’s box-office failure sharpens the debate over Tom Cruise’s climate satire
content.shortHeadline: Digger flops as critics split over Cruise’s climate satire
content.standfirst: Alejandro G Iñárritu’s film opened to $20m worldwide against reported production and marketing costs far higher. Critics disagree over whether its deliberately awkward performance and theatrical reveal add up to an audacious work or a failed experiment.

image.caption: Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell and Riz Ahmed as Dr Nirav Ganesh in Digger.

sources.originalTitle: Digger may lose $150m after Tom Cruise film bombs at the box office
Tom Cruise’s Digger has flopped spectacularly – but I think it is a misunderstood masterpiece
Tom Cruise has forgotten how to act
Digger review: Tom Cruise takes the 'biggest risk of his career' in this 'love-it-or-hate-it' folly ★★★★☆

segments.body: Digger took $20m globally in its opening weekend, including $8m in North America, according to the box-office report. Its production budget has been reported at between $125m and $150m, with marketing estimated at a further $100m; one projection put the potential loss at about $150m. The weak debut follows a heavily criticised release and leaves the film far short of its awards-season ambitions.

segments.title: A reveal that divides critics
segments.body: The film’s central twist reframes Tom Cruise’s oil tycoon as an actor performing in a play about climate catastrophe. One critic argues the reveal makes Digger a sharp question about art, reality and the limits of satire; another finds Cruise’s performance too self-conscious to persuade. The BBC review calls the film an eccentric, politically blunt folly and praises its ambition, while acknowledging its excesses.

perspectives.body: The BBC review embraces Digger as a risky, conceptually challenging eco-satire, arguing that Cruise’s commitment and the film’s environmental message make its excesses worthwhile.

content.headline: Sense and Sensibility’s new adaptation prompts debate over Austen’s heroines
content.shortHeadline: A new Sense and Sensibility puts Austen’s heroines in focus
content.standfirst: Georgia Oakley’s film brings fresh attention to Elinor and Marianne, while critics and experts debate what screen versions gain—and lose—when they emphasise romance, looks and visual atmosphere over Austen’s social observation.

image.caption: Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood in Georgia Oakley’s adaptation.

sources.originalTitle: Every millennial should read Sense and Sensibility
Fiona Shaw: ‘They didn’t think women were funny when I was young’
'The 21st-Century gym-toned bodies put me out': Four things Jane Austen adaptations get wrong - according to experts

segments.body: The new Sense and Sensibility, starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles, is darker and less glossy than the much-loved 1995 version, according to the review. Its story of two sisters negotiating money, love and social expectations also invites a modern reading: the tension between guardedness and emotional excess still feels familiar in a culture shaped by public sharing and uncertain prospects.

segments.title: What adaptations can leave behind
segments.body: A discussion with Austen specialists argues that adaptations can make romance the main event at the expense of class and women’s financial insecurity, while modern beauty standards and reduced dialogue can flatten the novels’ subtleties. Fiona Shaw, who plays Mrs Jennings, describes Oakley’s approach as pared back; she also sees her character as performing a role while remaining essentially benign.

perspectives.body: The experts’ criticism is not a demand for literal fidelity: they focus on what screen versions may lose when Austen’s irony, conversational detail and social critique give way to romantic imagery.

content.headline: Comédie Française turns backstage Macbeth chaos into a brisk French farce
content.shortHeadline: Comédie Française makes pre-show Macbeth chaos funny
content.standfirst: A run of mishaps threatens to derail opening night, leaving the director to take over as Lady Macbeth. The review praises the performers’ comic timing while finding the film’s career-and-motherhood subplot less convincing.

image.caption: A scene from Comédie Française.

sources.originalTitle: Comédie Française review – pre-show bedlam plays theatrical chaos for laughs

segments.body: The film unfolds in the three hours before a Paris production of Macbeth is due to open. Its director, Nina, arrives without her staff pass and faces a mounting list of problems: missing performers, superstitious actors, technical obstacles and an absent Lady Macbeth. The review calls the French farce a hoot, especially as Nina is forced to consider stepping into the role herself.

The comic mayhem includes a stoned grande dame, rehearsal-time infidelity and a stage manager who explains in exhaustive detail why each problem cannot be solved. The review finds the cast’s timing and its portrait of theatrical egos consistently enjoyable, though it is less persuaded by the subplot about Nina balancing motherhood with her career.

content.headline: Behemoth! lets a gifted cello player drift through an unfocused drama
content.shortHeadline: Behemoth! is undone by its wandering structure
content.standfirst: Tony Gilroy’s first feature in years has an intriguing musical setting and a strong cast, but its shifting timelines, subplots and styles leave the film without a compelling centre, according to the review.

image.caption: Pedro Pascal in Behemoth!.

sources.originalTitle: Behemoth! review - Pedro Pascal classical music drama hits all the wrong notes

segments.body: Pedro Pascal plays Alex, a cello virtuoso who returns to Los Angeles for session work and to be near his family. He is haunted by a past affair with a violinist and becomes preoccupied with her daughter, a teenage musical prodigy. The review sees promise in the premise and the film’s musical world, but says a disorienting structure prevents its parts from coming together.

segments.title: A drama without an anchor
segments.body: The film moves from grief and yearning to action scenes, with flashbacks and subplots that the review finds insufficiently developed. Eva Victor’s performance is singled out as a bright spot, while Pascal’s Alex is judged too distant from his own life to hold the story together. The result, in the critic’s view, is a film that gestures toward weighty themes without making them resonate.

content.headline: The Yellow Tie follows a conductor who insisted music must be heard live
content.shortHeadline: The Yellow Tie profiles a conductor opposed to recordings
content.standfirst: John Malkovich plays Sergiu Celibidache in a family-directed biopic about the celebrated conductor’s refusal to record music. The review finds a sturdy, heartfelt film, though it questions the force of its central argument.

image.caption: John Malkovich in The Yellow Tie.

sources.originalTitle: The Yellow Tie review – John Malkovich gives major hauteur as legendary record-hating maestro

segments.body: Sergiu Celibidache believed recorded music was inert and that a performance mattered because it happened in the moment. The Yellow Tie follows his rise from a young musician in Nazi-era Berlin to principal conductor of the Berlin Philharmonic after the war, and then through a wandering career across Europe and Latin America.

Directed by Celibidache’s son, the film is described as robust and heartfelt, with John Malkovich playing the older conductor and Ben Schnetzer the younger one. The review sees a lonely heroism in Celibidache’s insistence on live performance, but wonders what the film makes of a position that gathered few followers in a music world full of equally principled musicians who disagreed.

content.headline: Karl Lagerfeld’s public persona still eludes this authorised documentary
content.shortHeadline: Karl Lagerfeld remains elusive in a dutiful documentary
content.standfirst: Nick Hooker’s film draws on the designer’s biography and access to people around him, but the review finds that it rarely gets beneath his carefully managed image or examines his controversies in depth.

image.caption: Karl Lagerfeld in his signature style.

sources.originalTitle: Karl review – straightforward tribute tells inside story of fashion world’s great eccentric Karl Lagerfeld

segments.body: Karl draws on William Middleton’s biography and interviews with Lagerfeld’s inner circle, alongside archive footage. It recalls his reinvention of Chanel and his later celebrity, while acknowledging how closely he guarded his private self. The review says that access to associates does not necessarily reveal the man behind the dark glasses and carefully delivered wit.

The documentary’s most revealing testimony comes from long-serving collaborators, including seamstress and adviser Amanda Harlech, rather than Lagerfeld’s famous friends. The review also notes that a brief reference to his controversial fatphobic comments is quickly passed over. It judges the film diligent but not definitive.

content.headline: James Dean’s fame hid the vulnerable young actor behind the icon
content.shortHeadline: Remembering the vulnerable actor behind James Dean’s icon
content.standfirst: A close reading of Dean’s brief career looks beyond the rebellious image to a performer frightened by sudden fame. His most affecting screen moment, the review argues, is one of need rather than cool.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: James Dean’s three leading film roles came in a career cut short by his death at 24. The article traces his work with director Elia Kazan, who drew on Dean’s strained relationship with his father when shaping Cal in East of Eden. It also considers how comparisons with Marlon Brando obscured the differences in their acting styles.

Dean’s image as a photogenic rebel was amplified after his death, but the piece argues that his vulnerability remains visible in East of Eden. Its final example is the unscripted moment when Cal embraces his father after a rejection: rather than the cool icon, the article sees a desperate young man reaching for affection.

content.headline: The Reluctant Vampire makes Eric Morecambe’s children’s books a family comedy
content.shortHeadline: The Reluctant Vampire is a comic treat for all ages
content.standfirst: Lenny Rush leads a warm, joke-packed adaptation about a human boy raised by vampires. The review praises its ensemble and the writing team’s affection for Morecambe’s books; Rush sees the story as a comic take on belonging.

image.caption: Lenny Rush as Valentine in The Reluctant Vampire.

sources.originalTitle: The Reluctant Vampire review – Lenny Rush’s absolute joy of a comedy is perfectly cast
Fangs a million: Lenny Rush on turning an Eric Morecambe classic into a hilarious vampire comedy

segments.body: Valentine is the second son in a vampire family, but he has no fangs, dislikes blood and cannot fly. The truth is that Valeeta rescued him as a human baby and brought him up as her own. The six-part adaptation of Eric Morecambe’s children’s books follows the family’s efforts to conceal that secret, with a new friendship adding to Valentine’s complicated life.

segments.title: Comedy with a sense of belonging
segments.body: The review celebrates Lenny Rush’s performance and a supporting cast that includes Tom Davis, Sian Clifford, Bill Bailey and Ross Noble. Rush describes the story as a universal teenage struggle to fit in, despite its vampires and gargoyles. He also says the show is intended for everyone, not only children.

perspectives.body: Rush sees Valentine’s difference as a metaphor for wondering whether you are doing things right or are good enough. He says hearing from families whose disabled children felt encouraged by his work has been a welcome, unexpected effect.

content.headline: Richard E Grant’s Traitors blunder and Ross Kemp’s paranoia set an unruly tone
content.shortHeadline: A Traitors confession and Ross Kemp’s nerves shake the castle
content.standfirst: Richard E Grant told a fellow player he was a Traitor almost as soon as he was chosen, while Ross Kemp turned innocent gestures into signs of danger. The opening episode’s mistakes may be just what makes this celebrity series compelling.

image.caption: Richard E Grant in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Richard E Grant has already ruined The Celebrity Traitors. It’s brilliant
Ross Kemp’s Traitors paranoia will be the Faithfuls’ downfall

segments.body: Richard E Grant’s apparent slip came moments after he and Maya Jama were chosen as Traitors: asked directly by Joe Lycett, Grant said he was one. The review reports that the producers and players were left unsure whether it was a blunder or a double bluff. It concludes that the confession’s confusion gives the new series an unusually dramatic launch.

segments.title: Suspicion can turn inward
segments.body: Ross Kemp, a Faithful, suspects Bella Ramsey after a harmless gesture and then worries that Leigh-Anne Pinnock has marked him for murder. The accompanying analysis argues that his vocal paranoia risks drawing attention and spreading false leads among the Faithful. It also notes the Traitors’ decision to use Kemp in a mission that could make him look suspicious.

perspectives.body: The analysis reads Kemp’s anxious play as a possible response to his tough public image: he may fear being humiliated, but saying every suspicion aloud is making him look more vulnerable.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after its latest revival stalls
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future after its latest revival
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its Disney+ partnership, cancelled a planned Christmas special and has no current Doctor. Fans and former contributors disagree on what went wrong, but hope the long-running series can return without losing its core values.

image.caption: Illustrations of several Doctor Who incarnations, including Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has been off screen since its 2025 series, and the BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+. A planned Christmas special has been cancelled, the show has no current Doctor, and the corporation is seeking a new funding partner. No one has yet stepped forward, leaving the series’ immediate future unclear.

segments.title: What comes next?
segments.body: The article traces the show’s past revivals and reinventions, from its 2005 return to the contested casting of its most recent Doctors. Contributors raise different concerns: Frank Skinner wants the BBC to act faster, while writer Nina Metivier points to the show’s traditions of kindness and curiosity. Others question whether scripts and the funding strategy served the programme.

perspectives.body: Skinner argues that Doctor Who did not need a huge Disney+ investment simply to tell a good story and worries about how long it has been kept off air. Scriptwriter Nina Metivier describes kindness and curiosity as values at its core.

content.headline: Friday Night Lights made small-town Texas football a story about people
content.shortHeadline: Friday Night Lights found humanity beyond the football field
content.standfirst: Twenty years on, the drama’s improvisational style, ensemble and close sense of place still stand out. Its world was shaped by a book about the costs and expectations surrounding high-school football in Texas.

image.caption: Connie Britton and Kyle Chandler in Friday Night Lights.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Brave from the beginning’: 20 years of Friday Night Lights – the sports drama that dared to be different

segments.body: Set in Dillon, Texas, Friday Night Lights centred on high-school football but drew on H. G. Bissinger’s reporting about Odessa and the pressures surrounding the sport. The series showed a town where games shaped the week, while also reflecting the racism, strained school resources and broken ambitions described in the book.

segments.title: A naturalistic ensemble
segments.body: Director Peter Berg encouraged actors to improvise and used handheld cameras, helping conversations feel less scripted. The show also gave its women characters lives beyond football and launched or advanced careers including Jesse Plemons and Michael B. Jordan. Despite narrative missteps, the article argues, its humanity and precise sense of place kept it grounded.

content.headline: The Split-Up brings a British Asian family into the centre of a glossy legal
content.shortHeadline: The Split-Up puts a British Asian family at its centre
content.standfirst: The Manchester-set spin-off carries forward The Split’s family and divorce-court drama with a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team. Its creators describe that everyday representation as a deliberate choice.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split-Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split-Up follows Aria Kishan, a barrister preparing to take over her family’s Manchester firm, until her mother’s death changes her father’s succession plans. A former partner joins the firm, and the six-part series pairs divorce cases with conflict inside the family. Ritu Arya says the role felt like a full-circle moment after growing up inspired by Goodness Gracious Me.

segments.title: Representation as ordinary life
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted British Asian characters living everyday lives rather than being defined by exceptional circumstances. Executive producer Abi Morgan says the spin-off keeps the original’s focus on family, love and betrayal while giving a new writing team room to shape it. Arya also describes researching the work of family lawyers for her role.

perspectives.body: Sarma says the series could not represent every part of British Asian culture; her aim was to create one family she recognised as contemporary and real, rather than a token version of a whole community.

content.headline: 70 Up ends a decades-long portrait of lives—and the camera’s influence
content.shortHeadline: 70 Up closes a life-spanning documentary experiment
content.standfirst: The final chapter of the series begun as Seven Up! revisits its participants and the choices that shaped their lives. It also makes space for criticism from some contributors about the way director Michael Apted portrayed them.

image.caption: Participants in the Seven Up! documentary series as children.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A little pill of poison’: Why the cast of 70 Up came to resent it

segments.body: The series began in 1964 by asking 14 seven-year-olds from different backgrounds what they thought their futures might hold. It returned to many of them every seven years, following changes in work, family and circumstance. With 70 Up, producers say, the experiment reaches its intended ending rather than continuing until only one participant remains.

segments.title: Who controls the portrait?
segments.body: The finale revisits criticism that the series’ interviews and editing sometimes narrowed participants into types. Peter Davies says he left after tabloid attacks on his comments about Margaret Thatcher, then returned years later partly to promote his writing and music. Others questioned whether Apted’s questions reflected assumptions about class and gender; the producer argues the participants and programme maintained trust.

perspectives.body: Davies says he is glad to have taken part but notes that there is always more to a person than a few hours of television can show. He does not feel sadness about the series ending and thinks it is the right time.

content.headline: Nigella Lawson’s Bake Off judging offers a welcome rejection of food guilt
content.shortHeadline: Nigella Lawson brings unapologetic pleasure to Bake Off
content.standfirst: The new judge’s delight in biscuits and objection to calling food “naughty” make a pointed contrast with calorie-conscious food talk. The review sees her approach as a refreshing presence on mainstream television.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson judges on The Great British Bake Off.

sources.originalTitle: Nigella is dismantling skinny culture one ‘naughty cookie’ at a time

segments.body: Nigella Lawson has brought an unguarded enjoyment of food to The Great British Bake Off, the review argues. When fellow judge Paul Hollywood described a contestant’s cookies as “naughty”, Lawson objected: “I don’t approve of talking about food as naughty. We need to take our pleasures where we can in life.”

The article contrasts Lawson’s approach with a wider culture of calorie counting and weight-loss marketing, and with the language of whether a treat is “worth the calories”. It argues that her visible pleasure in baking and eating offers a welcome alternative, while making clear that this is the writer’s response to her role on the show.

content.headline: Damilola Taylor’s story gets a moving account from people who knew him
content.shortHeadline: A new film honours Damilola Taylor through those who knew him
content.standfirst: Friends, family and people involved in the case revisit the killing of the ten-year-old and its aftermath. The programme also asks why similar deaths occurred, holding onto grief while finding room for hope in his legacy.

image.caption: Damilola: The Untold Story on BBC Two.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: an essential film about the story of Damilola Taylor

segments.body: Damilola: The Untold Story brings together people who knew the ten-year-old, including actor John Boyega and his sister Grace, who were with Damilola at the library shortly before his death. His brother Tunde and caretaker Guillermo Casal also revisit the events that led to the conviction of two brothers.

The television recommendation describes the programme’s trauma and sadness as palpable, but says it also finds love and hope in Damilola’s legacy. It broadens its view from the case to ask why there were so many similar killings, while giving those closest to him the chance to tell their account.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day’s excellent combat can’t save a repetitive prequel
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day has thrilling combat but little else
content.standfirst: The prequel returns to the series’ alien invasion and delivers its most satisfying combat in years. But recycled routes, overstuffed maps and disruptive collectibles make the surrounding campaign feel safe and drawn out.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: E-Day depicts the invasion that has haunted the Gears of War series, with Marcus Fenix and a mismatched squad caught in a city under attack.
